title: Import tariff on domestic firm investment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
We will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal effect of the 2018 steel/aluminum tariff on capital investment at U.S. domestic steel producers compared to non-metals manufacturers. The DID method is appropriate here because we have a treatment group (steel producers) and a control group (non-metals manufacturers), and we can compare the change in capital investment before and after the tariff for both groups.

The key assumption in DID is that, in the absence of the treatment, the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend. In other words, the parallel trends assumption must hold.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(plm)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s06_data.csv")

# Convert period and treated to factors
data$period <- as.factor(data$period)
data$treated <- as.factor(data$treated)

# Estimate the DID model using fixed effects
fe_model <- plm(y ~ treat_x_post, data = data, model = "within")

# Print the coefficient for treat_x_post
summary(fe_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Estimate"]

# Robustness check: cluster-robust standard errors
coeftest(fe_model, vcovHC(fe_model, type = "HC1"))

# Event study plot
data$treatment_effect <- as.numeric(data$post) - as.numeric(data$treated) * 4
plot(data$treatment_effect, data$y, xlab = "Quarters relative to tariff", ylab = "Log Capital Expenditure", main = "Event Study Plot")
abline(h = mean(data$y), col = "red", lty = 2)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect the coefficient on `treat_x_post` to be positive, indicating that the 2018 steel/aluminum tariff led to an increase in capital investment at U.S. domestic steel producers compared to non-metals manufacturers. The magnitude of the effect will depend on the data, but we expect it to be economically significant given the potential impact of the tariff on the steel industry. The parallel trends assumption should hold if there were no other major policy changes or economic shocks affecting the steel and non-metals sectors around the same time.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=protected sector firms, control=unaffected manufacturers
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Tariff-protected firms increase capex relative to non-protected peers
_ground_truth.main_effect: 22% higher investment in treated firms post-tariff
